newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan key discount rate seen steady in 1996/97.
newsitem.headline: Japan key discount rate seen steady in 1996/97.

text.p: Japan's official discount rate is likely remain steady this business year, but the nation's key long-term interest rate is expected to rise, leading economists predicted in a Reuters poll issued on Thursday.
Economists at 30 banks, securities firms and research institutions in Tokyo and London were polled between October 15 and 17 on the Japanese economy, although not all responded to all the questions.

Of the 23 economists who commented on Japan's official discount rate, all said they expected Japan's official discount rate (ODR) to remain steady at the current 0.50 percent at least for the rest of 1996.
Almost all thought the rate would stay unchanged at least until the beginning of the next business year in April.
Two economists saw the ODR rising to 0.75 percent sometime between January and March 1997.

The average of the forecasts by 24 economists on the key long-term market interest rate during the last quarter of this calendar year was 3.05 percent. The yield of the 182nd cash bond was at around 2.690 percent on Thursday.
The economists, on average, predicted that the rate would rise to 3.22 percent between January and March 1997.
Mamoru Yamaguchi, an economist at Nikko Research Center, said he expected the long-term interest rate to rise to 3.0 percent in the first quarter of the 1997 calendar year.

"Taking into account that JGB issues will have to be increased for next fiscal year's budget in order to pay off interest on government debt, I think there will be upward pressure on the long-term interest rate," Yamaguchi said.
Yasuhiko Ushikubo, an economist at the Industrial Bank of Japan, said the key long-term interest rate is currently too low and does not reflect economic fundamentals.

"There are expectations among dealers that agricultural financial institutions will buy JGBs with the funds they get back as part of a government scheme to bail out failed mortgage firms," Ushikubo said.
Such expectations are supporting the JGB market and have helped to drive the benchmark yield down, he said.

Bond traders say agricultural financial institutions are expected to receive 2.7 trillion yen ($24.1 billion), possibly in late November, as part of a government plan to solve the problem of bad loans at failed mortgage firms. Financial institutions have contributed to a pool of funds, which will be invested, and the profits will be used to dispose of the loans.

Once the excitement surrounding the possibility of a cash flow into the JGB market calms down, the yield of the benchmark 182nd cash JGB will probably return to around three percent, which would more accurately reflect current economic fundamentals, IBJ's Ushikubo said.
"The economy is recovering gradually overall, and I expect no large change in the Bank of Japan's monetary policy for the time being," he added.
Nikko's Yamaguchi said the BOJ would probably have to continue to support the feeble economy by maintaining its current policy of keeping interest rates low.
"The Ministry of Finance has not changed its cautious stance on increasing government spending, which means support for the economy will have to come by way of monetary policy," Yamaguchi said.
